blocks.text: Walk through a village market where forty women sell the same white garri from identical basins. Ask one of them to charge ₦100 more than her neighbours and she will laugh at you — she would not sell a cup. She is a price taker, and her market is the closest thing in real life to perfect competition.

blocks.markdown:
**Market structure** describes the way a market is organised: how many firms there are, whether the product is identical across sellers, how easily new firms can enter, and how much control any one firm has over price. Economists distinguish four structures — perfect competition, monopoly, monopolistic competition and oligopoly.

**Perfect competition** is the theoretical benchmark against which the others are judged. It rarely exists in pure form, but it shows what a market would look like if competition were complete.

items: **Many buyers and many sellers**, each too small to influence the market price.
**A homogeneous product** — the goods of every seller are identical, so buyers have no reason to prefer one seller.
**Free entry into and exit from the industry** — no legal, technical or financial barriers.
**Perfect knowledge** — buyers and sellers know the ruling price everywhere in the market.
**Perfect mobility of factors of production** between uses.
**No transport costs**, so the price is the same throughout the market.
**No government interference** and no collusion between sellers.
**Independent decision making** by every buyer and seller.

blocks.title: Price taker
blocks.text: A firm that must accept the ruling market price because its own output is too small a share of total supply to affect it. Its demand curve is therefore a horizontal straight line at the market price, and average revenue equals marginal revenue equals price. If it raises its price it sells nothing; if it lowers it, it gives away revenue for no reason.

blocks.markdown:
### Equilibrium of the firm

A perfectly competitive firm maximises profit where **marginal cost equals marginal revenue**, and since MR equals price, the condition is **MC = price**.

In the **short run** the firm may earn abnormal profit if price exceeds average total cost, break even if the two are equal, or make a loss if price is below average total cost. It will keep producing at a loss so long as price covers average variable cost, because it is at least contributing something towards its fixed costs. If price falls below average variable cost it shuts down.

In the **long run** free entry and exit remove abnormal profits. If existing firms are earning abnormal profit, new firms enter, market supply rises, price falls. If firms are making losses, some leave, supply falls, price rises. Equilibrium is reached where **price equals minimum average total cost**, so every firm earns only **normal profit** — just enough to keep it in the industry.

blocks.caption: A price taker facing a market price of ₦150. Profit peaks at ₦100 when 5 units are produced, the last output for which marginal cost is still below ₦150

blocks.title: Proving the profit-maximising output for a price taker
blocks.prompt: Using the table above, show why 5 units and not 4 or 6 is the equilibrium output, and state the profit.

steps.text: Because the firm is a price taker, every extra unit sold brings in exactly ₦150, so MR = ₦150 at all outputs.
The fifth unit costs ₦130 to produce and earns ₦150, so it adds ₦20 to profit. Produce it.
The sixth unit costs ₦210 and earns ₦150, so it subtracts ₦60 from profit. Do not produce it.
Confirm with the profit column: ₦80 at 4 units, ₦100 at 5 units, ₦40 at 6 units. The maximum is at 5 units.

Equilibrium output is therefore 5 units with profit of ₦100. Since price of ₦150 exceeds average total cost of ₦650 ÷ 5 = ₦130, this is abnormal profit — which in the long run would attract new entrants and be competed away.

blocks.answer: Equilibrium output is 5 units, with abnormal profit of ₦100 that free entry would eliminate in the long run

blocks.title: Normal profit is not zero profit in the ordinary sense
blocks.text: Normal profit is the minimum return that keeps the entrepreneur in the industry — it is counted as a cost of production. Saying a firm in long-run perfect competition earns "no profit at all" loses the mark. Say it earns normal profit only, because abnormal profit has been competed away by new entrants.

points: Market structure describes the number of firms, product homogeneity, ease of entry and degree of price control.
Perfect competition assumes many buyers and sellers, a homogeneous product, free entry, perfect knowledge, factor mobility and no transport costs.
A perfectly competitive firm is a price taker whose demand curve is horizontal, so average revenue equals marginal revenue equals price.
Equilibrium output is where marginal cost equals price.
In the short run abnormal profit or loss is possible; a firm shuts down only when price falls below average variable cost.
In the long run free entry and exit reduce profit to normal profit, with price equal to minimum average total cost.
